lesson.title: The Information Highway Between Brain and Body
lesson.summary: The spinal cord is the central nervous system's main relay pathway, a bundle of neural tissue running through the vertebral column that carries signals to and from the brain while also managing certain reflexes on its own.
lesson.body:
The central nervous system consists of just two structures: the brain and the spinal cord. If the brain is the body's command center, the spinal cord is the highway that carries nearly all the traffic between that command center and everywhere else. It is a long bundle of neural tissue, about as thick as a finger, that runs down the length of the vertebral column, protected by the bony vertebrae that surround it. Beyond the vertebrae themselves, three layers of connective tissue called the meninges, along with a cushioning layer of cerebrospinal fluid, provide additional protection against injury.

In cross section, the spinal cord has a distinctive structure. At its core is an H-shaped region of gray matter, made up of neuron cell bodies and short interneurons that process and relay signals locally. Surrounding this gray matter is white matter, made up of long, myelinated axons bundled into tracts. Ascending tracts carry sensory information up toward the brain, while descending tracts carry motor commands down from the brain toward the muscles. This layered organization is what allows the spinal cord to function simultaneously as a conduction pathway and a local processing center. Two well known examples are the corticospinal tract, which carries voluntary motor commands down from the cortex, and the spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature information up toward the thalamus.

Because sensory and motor tracts both pass through the spinal cord, damage at any given level can interrupt communication between the brain and everything below that point, even though the tissue above and below the injury may be perfectly healthy. This is why the location of a spinal cord injury matters so much clinically: an injury high in the neck can affect breathing and all four limbs, while an injury lower in the back may leave arm function intact but affect only the legs. This segmental organization mirrors the fact that groups of spinal nerves exit at different levels to serve different regions of the body.

The spinal cord does not simply pass messages along, it can also act on its own. Reflexes, like the knee-jerk response a doctor tests with a small rubber hammer, are processed largely within the spinal cord: a sensory neuron detects the stretch in the tendon, a synapse relays the signal, and a motor neuron fires back out to contract the muscle, all before the signal has even reached the brain. This is why reflexes are so fast and why a person can still show some reflexes even when the brain is not conscious.

The spinal cord's motor output ultimately reaches the skeletal muscles through the somatic nervous system, and its sensory input arrives from those same somatic pathways carrying signals from the skin and joints. Without the spinal cord serving as the relay point between these peripheral pathways and the brain, none of that sensory and motor traffic would have anywhere to go.
